# RBE 549, Week 7 Assignment Report

Tom Kazakov

*Lab summary: detect, recognize, and tally the values of the US coins using Hough circles and other algorithms explored in the course.*  
*![][image1]*  
*Figure 1\. Final outcome, tally of the coin values*

# General Approach Summary

1. Detect the coins with Hough circles. Tune Hough parameters visually for the most stable detection. Calibrate the pixel-to-mm ratio for the given camera field of view. Compare the detected size to the reference chart (validated by US Treasury data and measurements of the coin samples on hand).  
2. Add color determination to reliably differentiate coins of similar size (primarily pennies and dimes). For repeatable white balance and exposure environment, produce a light-controlled enclosure.  
3. Add feature learning on identified samples and feature detection mode as a supplement to the size- and color-based recognition.  
4. Pickle tuning, calibration, and learned features to persist the state with minimal infrastructure.  
5. Add temporal filtering to reduce jitter in detection and recognition. Run expensive feature detection off established coin presence. 

# Enclosure

Very quickly after the start of work on this project, it became apparent that the lighting variation in my office is way too drastic. There are conflicting light temperatures from the natural light, overhead lights, and desk lamp. To produce a stable environment with a controlled field of view and lighting, an enclosure was needed.

# Implementation Milestones

1. Application scaffold and untuned Hough circle detection.  
2. Tune mode and picking setup.  
3. Calibration and size-based classification.  
4. Color analysis and fused recognition (size \+ color decision tree).  
5. Temporal smoothing to reduce jitter.  
6. SIFT feature detection biases recognition when confidence is high.  
7. Tally mode, acceptance testing, polish.

# Application Flow

1. Every frame, run cv2.HoughCircles on a median-blurred grayscale image from the camera feed. Outputs the list of (x, y, r).   
2. Tally mode. Each circle gets three classifiers:   
   1. size (pixel radius multiplied by the calibrated scale factor; outputs the coin with the closest Treasury diameter),   
   2. color (mean HSV in 80%-shrunk circular ROI determines silver/copper/gold by saturation, then hue),   
   3. and fusion (size wins everywhere except penny/dime.   
3. Temporal smoothing: The Tracker class instance matches detections to existing tracks based on the nearest Euclidean distance (\<50px). Each track accumulates a sliding window of 15 observations.   
   1. The position is defined as the median of the coordinates.   
   2. The label is determined by a majority vote.   
   3. Tracks need 5 observations before appearing.  
   4. The detected coin is evicted after 5 frames of being unseen.   
4. SIFT pipeline: When a track's majority-vote label first stabilizes, or changes, a 60-frame (\~2s) timer starts. If the label holds, the track is queued for SIFT. One coin is processed per frame from the queue.   
   1. FLANN works against all learned descriptors per denomination.  
   2. Lowe's ratio test is applied to individual matches, then a 1.5x ratio gates whether the result biases the tracker or just appears as a diagnostic.  
5. Tune: Trackbars for Hough param1, param2, minRadius, maxRadius. Auto-saved to pickle on every change.  
6. Calibration mode: User places a known coin at the crosshairs (frame center, minimal lens distortion) and presses Space. Adaptive radius bounds replace trackbar values.  
7. Learn: Present coins of selected denomination, press Space. SIFT descriptors extracted at full radius, appended to feature database. Accumulative: never overwrites previously learned features (pickle file needs to be destroyed to start over).  
8. Persistence: Two pickle files: parameters (VisionCoin.pkl, saved on change) and features (VisionCoin\_features.pkl, saved on learn).

# Observations and Notes

1. I started with the adjustable arm holding the camera, and it became apparent very quickly that size calibration is essential. I’m implying calibrating against a coin in the center of the frame to reduce the effects of the lens distortion and geometric aberrations. Also, the lighting in the center of the field is the most uniform and will produce the sharpest edge contrast.  
2. The backdrop for the samples is my desk-size mousepad. It’s black and matte, and generally a good surface for reducing reflections and improving contrast, but in the production environment, I would experiment with different backdrop colors and materials.  
3. Some form of persistence is essential to the application design for this lab. I restarted the app, probably hundreds of times. It would be too cumbersome to recalibrate the app across runs. A simplistic approach to Hough parameters and size ratio would be to set the values and then adjust constants in the module, but I expected to need persistence for learned features either way, and pickle is the Pythonic way to approach the task.  
4. Based on the experiments, the best Hough parameter suite I produced was still insufficient to separate pennies from dimes because of only a 1.14mm size gap.   
5. BRIO has annoyingly coarse controls for focus and exposure. For this lab, I consistently wanted to use more typical DSLR ⅓ or ½ EV steps, as the image was either overexposed, losing color, or underexposed, losing detail definition.   
6. The focus was on addressing the enclosure height through careful measurements to stay within the acceptable DoF range for all coin types. Still, US coins have \~0.5mm of height difference from a penny to a dollar, which is pushing the DoF of BRIO. A production system would need better optics and more precise exposure control.  
7. Bias in the decision/fusion process was adjusted multiple times during app development. The resulting “size prevails for mostly everything” heuristic is possible because of how reliable size determination worked, as long as the coin is fully in the camera’s FoV.  
8. Hue and saturation values used for color determination are sufficiently distinct to enable reliable color grouping under controlled lighting conditions. I washed the coins used for this assignment in an ultrasonic cleaner with a general-purpose metal parts solvent, so the specimens are in quite a pristine state. In real-life situations, color determination could be hindered by discoloration or debris on the coins.  
9. Lighting for the enclosure took some thought and design. A ring light I started with was too harsh and too concentrated. The soft, lower-power LED strips were a good solution.  
10. OpenCV doesn’t have an option to remove trackbars once spawned. The window needs to be recreated to remove the trackbars. The annoying consequence was a corrupted screen recording after demonstrating toggling tune mode: macOS lost the context of the initially selected window, resulting in no output in the recording.   
11. The resulting code is a 900+ LoC monolith that does not follow best practices for maintainable Python code. One file is prescribed by the assignment, and this is acceptable for an experimental implementation, but production code should be better organized and more thoroughly covered by unit tests.

# Feature recognition

1. SIFT vs. SURF should be weighed more carefully for real-world applications. I went with SIFT for this experiment to enable more robust and precise feature matching, since performance was not a design requirement.  
2. I attempted a visual gallery of SIFT features, but a proper implementation (capturing thumbnails of the detected features) would have required too much effort relative to mostly curiosity-driven benefits.  
3. Feature recognition for more than one coin in view and for many samples learned produced a noticeable performance hit. Enough to trigger SIFT once the coin was reliably detected (a 2-second delay from first seen) and to process the coins in sequence.  
4. Overall, coins share many similar features and were not reliably detected. It also doesn’t help that heads and tails can have drastically different commemorative designs. In the final implementation, only matches with a top-to-second match ratio above a 1.5x threshold affect the denomination recognition.  
   ![][image5]  
   *Figure 4\. Matches across the library of learned features per denomination*    
5. After consulting with the professor, I explored two weaker aspects of the implementation: sample collection and constraining feature detection by the distance (similar to Lab 5).  
6. Carefully curating the sample set, selecting the most distinct faces of the same coin types, and avoiding duplicates yielded some marginal improvement. Unlike what I expected to find in an ML-based implementation, redundant samples immediately reduce feature matching quality for SIFT.  
7. Capturing the distance and discriminating against features outside the distance threshold helped somewhat, but the coins have way too many similar, non-descriptive features. A portrait on a quarter is not that different from a portrait on a dime.   
8. One hypothesis that could be explored for a real-world implementation would be taking macro pictures, with one coin face taking most of the sensor real estate. In that case, the pixel distance between features would be much greater than the field of view in this implementation, where several dozen coins can fit.   
9. Lastly, it would be interesting to develop a system where the user is presented with the feature choices, and they would only register the descriptive ones for a given denomination.

# Gen AI Usage

1. Claude Opus 4.6 for general conversational ideation, probing around assignment requirements, formulating approach & strategy. Doesn’t produce code. Does proofread my technical writing.   
2. For general code-writing, PyCharm with LLM-powered contextual suggestions, boilerplate writing, spellchecker, and linter.   
3. Claude Code in PyCharm for interactive code gen and refactoring; used Opus 4.6. All code produced by Gen AI for this assignment was reviewed and verified, and also refactored or recomposed to varying degrees. Commit history in the repo can serve as proof of organic authorship: [https://github.com/kzkv/RBE549/commits/main/](https://github.com/kzkv/RBE549/commits/main/)   
4. Multi-agent setup in Claude Code: non-specialist Claude to sequence implementation plan; Briefer serves as a conversation partner to discuss each increment step; Drafter produces initial code to be reviewed, refactored, and acceptance-tested; Critic observes the increment and provides feedback for the material. For consistency and to avoid re-setup costs, the instructions are stored in the repo-level CLAUDE.md file.
